book: 113 - Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required

chapters.relation: Editorial introduction tracing the successive identities of Johnny Allen Hendrix, James Marshall Hendrix, Jimmy James, and Jimi — from Seattle and the chitlin' circuit with the Isley Brothers and Little Richard to Chas Chandler's London — arguing there was no single Hendrix but a series of continual transformations. It dismisses a 'Hegelian unfolding of The Absolute' that would require true blues musicians to be born in the South, and speculates that the Jimi lost in 1970 was a would-be jazz-blues synthesizer, reading 'Rainy Day, Dream Away' and 'Still Raining, Still Dreaming' as evidence and invoking the rumored Miles Davis collaboration.

chapters.file: ch09 - 1. I Stand Up Next to a Mountain.md
chapters.relation: Reads Hendrix as Joseph Campbell's hero on the monomyth of separation, initiation, and return: the mother's death and gypsy prophecy of 'Voodoo Chile' stage the separation, the Venus witch's ring the initiation, and the transcending guitar solo the return, with Prometheus as the type of the fire-bringer punished by promoters, Little Richard, and audiences demanding the hits. Through Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy it casts the Monterey guitar-burning and the Dionysian intensity of the Experience as tragic art whose hero 'shoulders the whole Dionysiac world for us,' and closes with Aristotle's Politics on catharsis — 'Machine Gun''s sonic battle imagery as purgation that transforms violence into a cry for peace.

chapters.file: ch10 - 2. Zen and the Art of Guitar Burning.md
chapters.relation: Argues Hendrix's art worked like a Zen transmission outside words and doctrine: Nansen's cat, the Buddha's silent flower sermon, Zeami's hidden flower in Noh, and Linji burning the sutras frame the guitar-burning, playing with his teeth, and the backwards tape of 'Are You Experienced?' as skillful means that shock listeners out of dualistic discrimination into pure suchness. The Woodstock sequence — the 'Star-Spangled Banner' followed seamlessly by 'Purple Haze' and the 'Instrumental Solo' — is read as an eschatological passage from the death-symbolism of the national anthem to a Zen-like experiential beginning, with Hendrix acting as a Bodhisattva whose Stratocaster is the master's stick of compassion.

Contends that Hendrix's discord is philosophy-as-discord: 'I Don't Live Today' (the Native American dead-in-life), the Woodstock 'Star-Spangled Banner' with its bombs and sirens against sporting-event sentimentality, 'Machine Gun,' and 'House Burning Down' lacerate listeners so they actually feel war's atrocities instead of parroting patriotic clichés. Against this the chapter sets the oceanic, womb-like escape fantasies of '1983 (A Merman I Should Turn to Be)' and 'Valleys of Neptune,' treating them through Schopenhauer as metaphysical consolation, Marx's opiate, and Nietzsche's 'hangman's metaphysics,' and concludes that Hendrix finally refuses such world-denying illusions — and Heideggerian inauthentic withdrawal — in favor of existential engagement with suffering here and now.

The editor asks where Hendrix's 'bestness' lies by testing whether he was ever free: his songs demand freedom ('If 6 Was 9,' 'Stone Free,' 'Freedom,' 'Ezy Ryder') but never assert that the human condition is free, and his caffeine-style appetites, exploitative contracts, and management suggest determination rather than liberty. A detour through 'Hey Joe' as premeditated murder — compared with Othello and the Ice-T 'Cop Killer' affair — argues that fabricated narrators make it impossible to glean an artist's own moral sense from songs. He concludes that Hendrix's deepest mastery was the treatment of love, from 'The Wind Cries Mary' to 'Little Wing,' making him the sixties' most powerful spokesman for love rather than freedom, per the quoted 'when the power of love overcomes the love of power.'

chapters.file: ch13 - II. I Know I Gotta Die When It’s Time for Me to Die.md

chapters.relation: Traces 'genius' from the indwelling genie of an art to Goethe as the first person the public called a genius, then applies Kant's doctrine — the genius gives the rule to future art, produces what no determinate rule can govern, and cannot explain or teach what he does — to Jimi (having the Experience learn 'Sgt. Pepper' on one hearing to play it back to the Beatles three days after its release), Janis ('a victim of my own insides'), and Jim. Schopenhauer's dark side of genius — more mind than character, a will that 'affirms its own life by denying the life of others' — explains why the 27 Club burned out, and why we say 'Jimi lives' but 'Jim is still alive.'

chapters.file: ch15 - 6. Quicker than the Wink of an Eye.md
chapters.relation: Defends Hendrix against the Allan Bloom-style charge that sixties self-expression was mere decadence by reading his life as Charles Taylor's ideal of authenticity: self-determining freedom replacing the older external goods of Plato's Good, Aristotle's polis, or Aquinas's God. The biography — the broken home behind 'Castles Made of Sand,' the rolling-stone mobility Dylan anthemed, the London synthesis of blues, rock, soul, and jazz, 'Watchtower''s 'let us not talk falsely now,' and the accusations of race desertion answered by the Watts commitment and 'House Burning Down' — becomes the development of an authentic voice, closing with Cornel West's 'tragi-comic poet' and the humanist manifesto of 'Bold as Love.'

chapters.file: ch16 - 7. A Life Along the Watchtower.md
chapters.relation: Reads 'All Along the Watchtower' as a dialogue between the Joker's Sartrean being-and-nothingness ('none of them along the line know what any of it is worth') and the Thief's Heideggerian reply — being-toward-death, anticipatory resoluteness, care, and the fallen 'they.' It argues Hendrix lived this struggle: the mirror-smashing of 'A Room Full of Mirrors,' the unborn speaker of 'Belly Button Window' who will throw himself into the world rather than be thrown, and the 'Electric Church Music' built to cut through 'they'-thinking and return listeners to child-like authenticity. Gramsci's point that oppressor and oppressed alike internalize the oppressor's message names the hegemony Hendrix's third way — neither victim nor revolutionary — simply denies.

chapters.file: ch17 - III. Flotation Is Groovy, Even a Jellyfish Will Tell You That.md
ch18 - 8. Facing Up to the Realities.md
chapters.relation: Argues that 'Machine Gun' and its Berkeley introduction ('people... fighting wars... within themselves, not facing up to the realities') make Hendrix an existentialist: since existence precedes essence, each of us lives multiple realities we must author responsibly. The lyric variants diagnose Sartrean bad faith twice over — 'evil man make me kill ya' is the helplessness that denies freedom, 'fight like a farmer' the blame that locates failure out there — before the reprise's acceptance ('let your bullets fly like rain') and free judgment ('I know all the time you're wrong') achieve authenticity amid the solo's sonic battlefield.

Proposes an 'experientialism' — subjective conscious experience as fundamental reality, defended against eliminativists who would explain experience away as illusion — and finds its moral core in Martin Buber: the title song and 'May This Be Love' call the beloved out of an I-It world ('made out of gold and can't be sold') into reciprocal I-You relation ('take hold of my hand'), while 'The Wind Cries Mary,' 'Purple Haze,' and 'Manic Depression' lament love that is absent or unreciprocated. Experiences feel most intensely real, the chapter argues, when the Platonic order of love puts what matters most at stake — which is why kissing the sky, even without being kissed back, is worth recommending.

chapters.file: ch20 - 10. Hendrix Out of the Cave.md
chapters.relation: Scores 'Are You Experienced?' and 'Purple Haze' against the Allegory of the Cave: the backwards guitar and reversed cymbals are the painful, clumsy ascent from shadows toward the Form of the Good, with Hendrix as the initiator who must first drag the prisoner violently and then gently — 'come on across to me... we'll hold hands.' 'Purple Haze' becomes the midway delirium between cave and sun ('don't know if I'm coming up or down,' 'scuse me while I kiss the sky'), and the chapter concludes that the psychedelia is philosophical — consciousness opened by liberation from received opinion, not by LSD — warning the freed prisoner not to remain a pale copy of Plato or Hendrix.

chapters.file: ch22 - 11. Vibrations and Echoes Long Ago.md
chapters.relation: Argues Hendrix's sound was made with — not merely on — studio technology: Eddie Kramer's Olympic Studios innovations, in the lineage of the BBC Radiophonic Workshop, used feedback, varispeed, and backwards tape as performing instruments. Andy Clark and David Chalmers's extended mind thesis (Chalmers's own example is Hendrix's mind extending into his guitar) and Chalmers on Pokémon Go frame the analog recordings as a more immersive augmented reality than digital games, while Kittler's claim that media 'determine our situation' and the time-bending processes of 'Purple Haze' and 'Are You Experienced?' explain how listening disorients and enriches our perception of time and space.

chapters.file: ch23 - 12. The Broken Pieces of Yesterday’s Life.md
chapters.relation: Uses the flood of posthumous Hendrix releases — the dismal Lonnie Youngblood eight-track, 380-plus albums, the PPX litigations — to ask what we owe the dead and what access we may claim, weighing Kafka and Max Brod, Nietzsche's sister, Harper Lee's Go Set a Watchman, and Kundera's Mirek. It rejects the framing of conflicting rights: against the Cartesian picture of a hidden self the authors deploy Wittgenstein's beetle in the box — 'the human body is the best picture of the human soul' — to show that no one can fully control their public self, leaving only prudential discernment about which recordings should shape our image of the artist.

Flips Joel Rudinow's 'Can White People Sing the Blues?' to ask whether a very black musician can play a genre that by the late sixties had become white property. With Wittgenstein's family resemblance — musical kinds lack necessary and sufficient conditions — it traces rock's migration from Chuck Berry and the Sanctified churches to the Stones and Beatles, diagnosing the 'Jimi problem': his blackness rendered his rock inauthentic (Christgau's 'psychedelic Uncle Tom,' radio bans) at the same time as his rock rendered him inauthentically black. The chapter endorses Hendrix's own refusal of labels — 'You don't need labels, man' — as a caution against unreflective categorization.

chapters.file: ch25 - 14. Hendrix from the Bottom Up.md
chapters.relation: A rhythm-section-first ('bottom up') listening of Electric Ladyland and the Fillmore East Band of Gypsys shows Hendrix re-grounding his music in blues, R&B, and jazz time: Steve Winwood's organ anchoring 'Voodoo Chile,' Buddy Miles's shuffle freeing the vocal-like guitar of 'Rainy Day, Dream Away,' and the communally stretched measure before 'Power to Love.' Kant supplies the vocabulary — the 'mercenary art' of studio craft versus art, and the Transcendental Aesthetic and the sublime — for the claim that the Gypsys' collectively felt rift in time approaches a rock'n'roll sublime that is 'felt as exceptionally and undeniably bad ass.'

chapters.file: ch26 - 15. You Can’t Use My Name.md
chapters.relation: Recounts how Hendrix changed law twice: ExperienceHendrix v. PPX (the 'You can't use my name' tapes) imported the Wrotham Park/Blake standard so breach-of-contract damages can reflect the infringer's gains rather than the victim's losses, and Experience Hendrix v. Hendrixlicensing.com used Washington's Personality Rights Act to extend postmortem publicity rights beyond the state of domicile, raising the constitutional problems Rossi identifies. The chapter then reads the dispute over whether the Woodstock 'Star-Spangled Banner' is art or noise through legal realism versus natural law theory and legal positivism — law as what courts actually enforce — and through the Institutional Theory of Art, with a Wittgensteinian cluster definition marking the essentialist route that failed.

chapters.file: ch27 - V. What Any of It Is Worth.md
ch28 - 16. Artistic Expression in the Land of the Free.md
chapters.relation: Argues that Hendrix's Woodstock 'Star-Spangled Banner' links political and artistic freedom: Mill's On Liberty — the harm principle, liberty of tastes and pursuits, and originality against the despotism of custom — both protects and celebrates the performance, since disliking it is no ground for suppressing it. Tolstoy's What Is Art? then supplies the aesthetic verdict: art is the infection of others by sincerely, particularly, and clearly felt emotion, so the anthem, like Picasso's Guernica, is great art expressing bad feelings about Vietnam — unlike José Feliciano's sincere-but-vague ballad or Roseanne Barr's failed joke.

Reads Hendrix as a romantic idealist on a Platonic-Neoplatonic arc: 'Room Full of Mirrors' shatters the cave wall and its projections toward The One, whose presence is pursued through eros with the veiled Beloved of Plotinus — the semi-divine feminine of 'Little Wing,' 'One Rainy Wish,' and 'Angel.' Hegel's Zeitgeist and world-spirit then frame the planned First Rays of the New Rising Sun as music meant to carry humanity's collective evolution, with Hendrix as Hegel's 'spiritual workman' and self-described messenger ('I am only a messenger and you are a Sheep in the process of evolution').

chapters.file: ch30 - 18. Musical Order from Sonic Chaos.md
chapters.relation: Explains guitar feedback as a non-linear dynamical system — strings, amp, and room air feeding output back into input — so that at Woodstock the anthem's closing notes ('yet wave...') are pulled from thin air while the whammy bar works, and 'Foxey Lady''s rising feedback shows order stirring itself out of chaos. With Laplace's predictability undone by chaos theory and Lorenz's butterfly, the chapter frames Hendrix as having learned 'to play chaos,' and locates musical beauty — citing Aristotle on symmetry, Hutcheson's 'uniformity in variety,' and Wundt's arousal curve — at the unstable border between boring order and meaningless noise.

Maps Alexis Korner's 'primitivistic' Hendrix onto the pre-Socratic element theories: Thales's water returns in the submarine Atlantis of '1983' and 'Valleys of Neptune,' Anaximenes's rarefaction and condensation in the flight and storm imagery, and Empedocles's Love and Strife in the Monterey burning — a sacrifice motivated by love, set against the Strife of 'Machine Gun,' 'Izabella,' and 'House Burning Down.' Heraclitus's unity of opposites and logos explain the fire-water paradox lyrics ('that crying blue rain that's burning my eyes,' 'If 6 was 9'), while Berkeley's tree in the forest shows how the audible emerges from mere vibration, as musical sound emerges from feedback and noise.

A British music writer's memoir-historical corrective: the 'Swinging Sixties' existed only in west London while provincial Britain remained grey and make-do-and-mend, but the blues boom of Cream, Mayall, the Yardbirds, and the Animals prepared the seedbed into which Hendrix landed in 1966 — a 'quantum blues leap' that still felt familiar. With comparatively milder (if passive-aggressive) racism, Chas Chandler, Noel Redding, and Mitch Mitchell, five UK Top Twenty singles against one American hit, McCartney's Monterey recommendation, and Keith Altham's guitar-burning idea, it was Britain that set him on his way.

holes.name: Catharsis (purgation of emotion through art)
holes.what: Aristotle's notion (Politics 8.7) that intense music and tragedy purge pity, fear, and frenzy, giving listeners harmless delight, pleasurable relief, and a more balanced state.
holes.why: Chapter 9's closing section argues Hendrix's 'Machine Gun' and tragic-hero persona deliver exactly this Aristotelian catharsis to his audience, but taxonomy has no slug for it.

holes.name: The Hero's Journey (monomyth)
holes.what: Joseph Campbell's three-stage myth pattern — separation, initiation, return — in which the hero leaves ordinary life, wins special knowledge and power, and brings a boon back to the world.
holes.why: Chapter 9 structures Hendrix's life and the 'Voodoo Chile' songs around this monomyth, casting him as a Prometheus who brings the fire of music back from his journeys.

holes.name: Kant's Theory of Genius
holes.what: Kant's Critique of Judgment doctrine that genius is an inborn talent producing original, exemplary works which 'give the rule' to future art, without the genius being able to explain or teach how.
holes.why: Chapter 14's whole account of Jimi, Janis, and Jim runs on this doctrine — astonishment becoming admiration, the genius who cannot explain himself — which no existing slug covers.

holes.name: Friedrich Kittler
holes.what: German media theorist (1943–2011) who held that media technologies are not mere tools but 'determine our situation,' as in Gramophone, Film, Typewriter.
holes.why: Chapter 22 uses Kittler's media theory to frame Hendrix's studio innovations, explicitly contrasting it with Clark and Chalmers's extended mind thesis.

holes.name: Family Resemblance
holes.what: Wittgenstein's idea that concepts like 'game' have no necessary and sufficient conditions but are united by overlapping, criss-crossing similarities.
holes.why: Chapter 24 argues musical genres like rock are family-resemblance kinds, which is the backbone of its analysis of whether Jimi played rock.

holes.name: Philosophy of Law (positivism, natural law, legal realism)
holes.what: Theories of what makes law law: posited by duly authorized legislatures (positivism), measured against moral or natural standards (natural law), or simply whatever courts enforce (American legal realism and Critical Legal Studies).
holes.why: Chapter 26 explains Hendrix's two law-changing cases through exactly this clash of jurisprudential theories, including Holmes's bad-man theory.

holes.name: Institutional Theory of Art
holes.what: The view (associated with Danto and Dickie) that something is art when the art world — critics, museums, buyers and sellers — deems it so, rather than in virtue of intrinsic properties.
holes.why: Chapter 26 applies this theory to decide whether Hendrix's Woodstock 'Star-Spangled Banner' counts as art or mere noise.

holes.name: Leo Tolstoy
holes.what: Russian novelist-thinker whose What Is Art? defines art as the infection of others by sincerely felt emotion, judged by particularity, clarity, and sincerity rather than beauty.
holes.why: Chapter 28 leans on Tolstoy's criteria to argue Hendrix's anthem is great art expressing 'bad feelings' about Vietnam, explicitly compared to Picasso's Guernica.

holes.name: Chaos Theory and Emergence
holes.what: The study of non-linear dynamical systems where deterministic rules yield practical unpredictability (sensitive dependence, feedback loops) and order spontaneously self-organizes.
holes.why: Chapter 30 explains Hendrix's guitar feedback as an emergent, chaotic phenomenon and pits it against Laplacean predictability.

holes.name: Pre-Socratic Element Theories (arche)
holes.what: The early Greek monists' search for a first principle (arche): Thales's water, Anaximander's quality-less apeiron, Anaximenes's condensing and rarefying air, and Empedocles's four elements driven by Love and Strife.
holes.why: Chapter 31 maps Hendrix's water, air, and fire imagery onto these theories — none of which except Heraclitus has a taxonomy slug — including Empedoclean Love and Strife.
